words.definition: to weaken gradually or secretly; to damage the foundation of
words.nuance: Literally to dig beneath; harm that works from below.
examples: Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.
Leaked documents threatened to undermine the negotiations.

words.definition: to spoil or impair the quality or effectiveness of; to invalidate
words.nuance: In law, fraud can vitiate a contract, making it void.
examples: A single biased sample can vitiate an entire study.
Proof of fraud would vitiate the contract.

words.definition: to delay or prevent by obstructing; to hinder
words.nuance: Slows something down rather than stopping it outright.
examples: Heavy snow will impede travel across the pass.
Bureaucratic rules often impede innovation.

words.definition: to prevent someone from accomplishing something
words.nuance: Stops a plan or attempt from succeeding.
examples: Quick-thinking guards managed to thwart the robbery.
Bad weather may thwart our plans for a picnic.

words.definition: to prevent or hinder the progress of
words.nuance: Leaves someone stuck, with no way forward.
examples: High interest rates can stymie economic growth.
A missing permit continued to stymie the builders.

words.definition: to prevent or obstruct by taking action ahead of time
words.nuance: Acting first so something never happens.
examples: The company cut prices to forestall competition.
A quick apology may forestall a lawsuit.

words.definition: to prevent from happening; to make impossible
words.nuance: Rules something out in advance.
examples: His injury does not preclude a return later in the season.
The terms of the contract preclude any sale before 2030.

words.definition: to make a problem or bad situation worse
words.nuance: Always about something already bad.
examples: Cutting staff will only exacerbate the delays.
Scratching can exacerbate a rash.

words.definition: to make a problem or injury worse; informally, to annoy
words.nuance: On the GRE, expect the 'make worse' sense.
examples: Running on a sprained ankle will aggravate the injury.
Harsh words only aggravate the conflict.

words.definition: to pacify or placate someone by giving in to their demands
words.nuance: Often critical: appeasing an aggressor only invites more demands.
examples: The king tried to appease the rebels with lower taxes.
Nothing could appease the furious crowd.

words.definition: to stop someone from being angry; to win over or reconcile
words.nuance: Often through goodwill or compromise.
examples: The mediator worked to conciliate the two factions.
She offered a compromise to conciliate her critics.

words.definition: to make suffering, a deficiency, or a problem less severe
words.nuance: Lightens a burden without necessarily removing it.
examples: The medicine helped alleviate her pain.
New roads should alleviate traffic downtown.

words.definition: to make something bad less severe, serious, or painful
words.nuance: Mitigating circumstances lessen blame.
examples: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat.
Nothing could mitigate the damage done by the scandal.

words.definition: to make something bad or unsatisfactory better
words.nuance: Improves a bad situation rather than merely easing pain.
examples: The new policy aims to ameliorate conditions in the prisons.
Volunteers worked to ameliorate the effects of the flood.

words.definition: to make a disease or its symptoms less severe without curing it
words.nuance: Also: to make an offense seem less serious. Palliative care relieves symptoms.
examples: The drugs could palliate the symptoms but not cure the disease.
No excuse can palliate such cruelty.

words.definition: to waste something, especially money or time, recklessly
words.nuance: Also used for wasted chances and talents.
examples: He managed to squander his inheritance in two years.
Don't squander the chance to study abroad.

words.definition: to accuse or blame; to incriminate
words.nuance: The opposite of exculpate.
examples: The new evidence seemed to inculpate the butler.
He refused to inculpate his friends to save himself.

words.definition: to show or declare that someone is not guilty
words.nuance: From Latin culpa, 'blame' (as in culprit).
examples: The DNA results helped exculpate the accused man.
She tried to exculpate herself by blaming the software.

words.definition: to officially clear someone of blame or wrongdoing
words.nuance: Often the result of an official inquiry.
examples: The investigation will likely exonerate the pilot.
New evidence may exonerate prisoners convicted decades ago.

words.definition: to clear someone of blame or suspicion; to show to be right or justified
words.nuance: Often used when later events prove someone right.
examples: The final results seemed to vindicate her unpopular decision.
He hoped the trial would vindicate his reputation.

words.definition: to shock or excite someone into taking action
words.nuance: Also means to coat metal with zinc.
examples: The tragedy helped galvanize support for new safety laws.
A rousing speech can galvanize a weary team.

words.definition: to strongly encourage or urge someone to do something
words.nuance: Earnest, often public urging.
examples: Coaches exhort their players to give everything in the final minutes.
The pamphlet sought to exhort citizens to vote.

words.definition: to provoke or annoy someone so as to stimulate a reaction
words.nuance: A goad is a pointed stick for driving cattle.
examples: His friends tried to goad him into jumping off the bridge.
Don't let the critics goad you into a hasty reply.

words.definition: to encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior
words.nuance: Almost always about stirring up something bad.
examples: The speech was meant to incite a riot.
Posts that incite violence are removed from the site.

words.definition: not permanent; lasting only a short time
words.nuance: A formal near-synonym of transient.
examples: Most of the swings in the polls were transitory.
Youth is transitory, as everyone eventually learns.

words.definition: so lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring
words.nuance: Commonplace to the point of tedium.
examples: The movie's dialogue was painfully banal.
She turned a banal topic into a fascinating talk.

words.definition: overused and consequently of little import; lacking originality
words.nuance: Usually of phrases, ideas, and advice.
examples: 'Follow your dreams' is a trite piece of advice.
Avoid trite phrases in your college essay.

words.definition: lacking significance through having been overused
words.nuance: Worn out by repetition.
examples: The plot relied on a hackneyed twist the audience saw coming.
Critics found the song's lyrics hackneyed.

words.definition: lacking flavor, interest, or vigor
words.nuance: Used for food and for dull art or people.
examples: The soup was insipid and needed salt.
An insipid performance put the audience to sleep.

words.definition: offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging
words.nuance: Empty of ideas or substance.
examples: The talk show was full of vapid celebrity gossip.
His vapid smile suggested he had not been listening.

words.definition: lacking poetic beauty; commonplace and unimaginative
words.nuance: Ordinary rather than boring, though the two overlap.
examples: The poet made a prosaic subject, a parking lot, surprisingly beautiful.
The explanation for the strange lights turned out to be prosaic.

words.definition: unable to keep still or silent; restless; also, resistant to control
words.nuance: Two senses: fidgety, and stubbornly resisting control.
examples: The restive audience began to shuffle and whisper.
Months of shortages made the population restive.

words.definition: having or showing great energy or enthusiasm for a cause or goal
words.nuance: Can tip into fanaticism.
examples: The zealous volunteers knocked on every door in town.
A zealous prosecutor pursued the case for years.

words.definition: very enthusiastic or passionate
words.nuance: Warm devotion, from Latin for 'burning'.
examples: She is an ardent supporter of public libraries.
His ardent letters revealed a deep love.

words.definition: having or displaying a passionate intensity
words.nuance: Often of beliefs, hopes, and prayers.
examples: The crowd sang with fervent devotion.
It is my fervent hope that the talks succeed.

words.definition: having a keen interest in or enthusiasm for something
words.nuance: Usually of hobbies: an avid reader, an avid fan.
examples: He is an avid reader of mystery novels.
The avid fans camped outside the stadium overnight.

words.definition: showing a lack of courage or determination; timid
words.nuance: Literally 'small-souled'.
examples: The pusillanimous leaders refused to take a stand.
It was pusillanimous of him to blame his assistant.

words.definition: contemptibly lacking in courage; cowardly
words.nuance: Carries strong contempt.
examples: The craven deserter abandoned his unit.
Critics called the decision a craven surrender to pressure.

words.definition: showing or suffering from nervousness or a lack of confidence
words.nuance: Timid rather than contemptibly cowardly.
examples: The timorous child hid behind her mother.
A timorous voice asked whether the meeting was over.

words.definition: fearless; adventurous
words.nuance: Often of explorers and reporters.
examples: The intrepid explorer crossed the desert alone.
Only the most intrepid reporters stayed in the war zone.

words.definition: showing fearlessness and determination
words.nuance: Undiscouraged by danger or failure.
examples: The dauntless firefighters went back into the building.
Despite repeated failures, she remained dauntless.

words.definition: showing a willingness to take bold risks; also, impudent
words.nuance: Can be admiring (daring) or critical (shamelessly bold).
examples: The audacious plan called for climbing the peak in winter.
It was audacious of him to ask for a raise on his first day.

words.definition: acting or done quickly without thought or care; impulsive
words.nuance: Emotion and haste win over reflection.
examples: In an impetuous moment, he quit his job.
Her impetuous decision to buy the house surprised everyone.

words.definition: acting or done without careful consideration of the possible consequences
words.nuance: Also a noun for a skin irritation.
examples: It would be rash to sign the contract without reading it.
Investors regretted their rash decisions during the panic.

words.definition: something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected
words.nuance: Common in science passages.
examples: The cold summer was an anomaly in the warming trend.
Scientists investigated the anomaly in the data.

words.definition: a departure from what is normal or expected, typically an unwelcome one
words.nuance: Implies the departure is temporary or wrong.
examples: The poor exam score was an aberration for such a strong student.
Officials described the violence as an aberration.

words.definition: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
words.nuance: Originally someone who destroyed religious images.
examples: The young iconoclast challenged every rule of classical music.
As an iconoclast, she questioned the field's founding assumptions.

words.definition: an unorthodox or independent-minded person
words.nuance: Originally an unbranded calf.
examples: The senator was a maverick who often voted against her party.
Silicon Valley loves the image of the lone maverick.

words.definition: deriving ideas, style, or taste from a broad and diverse range of sources
words.nuance: Usually admiring.
examples: The café has an eclectic mix of furniture.
Her eclectic taste in music ranges from opera to punk.

words.definition: fond of company; sociable
words.nuance: Also used for animals that live in groups.
examples: The gregarious host introduced every guest to each other.
Wolves are gregarious animals that live in packs.

words.definition: friendly, lively, and enjoyable
words.nuance: Often of gatherings and atmospheres.
examples: The dinner was a convivial affair full of laughter.
He was a convivial host who kept everyone's glass full.

words.definition: friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to
words.nuance: Approachable warmth.
examples: The affable guide answered every question patiently.
Despite his fame, he remained affable and modest.

words.definition: a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality
words.nuance: Usually 'a paragon of' some virtue.
examples: She was a paragon of patience with her students.
The museum is a paragon of modern design.

words.definition: a person or thing serving as a typical or excellent example
words.nuance: A model to be copied.
examples: The bridge is an exemplar of Roman engineering.
Teachers held him up as an exemplar of good study habits.

words.definition: a person or thing that is a perfect example of a quality or type
words.nuance: Pronounced e-PIT-uh-mee.
examples: The hotel is the epitome of luxury.
He was the epitome of calm under pressure.

words.definition: the time at which something is most powerful or successful
words.nuance: Literally the point in the sky directly overhead.
examples: The empire reached its zenith in the second century.
At the zenith of her career, she starred in three films a year.

words.definition: the point at which something is at its best or most highly developed
words.nuance: The height of perfection.
examples: The cathedral represents the acme of Gothic architecture.
Many consider that album the acme of the band's career.

words.definition: the lowest point in the fortunes of a person or organization
words.nuance: The opposite of zenith.
examples: The team's nadir came with a ten-game losing streak.
At the nadir of the recession, one in ten workers was unemployed.

words.definition: a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases
words.nuance: Usually used to deny that something is one.
examples: Technology is not a panacea for poor teaching.
Some saw the new drug as a panacea.

words.definition: a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief
words.nuance: Slightly formal; also a new convert.
examples: The course is ideal for a neophyte with no coding experience.
As a political neophyte, she relied on her advisers.

words.definition: a person new to or inexperienced in a field or situation
words.nuance: The everyday word for a beginner.
examples: The ski slope is too steep for a novice.
Even a novice cook can follow this recipe.

words.definition: a beginner or novice
words.nuance: Rare and literary.
examples: The tyro made every mistake in the book during his first week.
Compared to her rivals, she was a tyro in politics.

words.definition: a person who cultivates an interest without real commitment or knowledge
words.nuance: Implies superficial dabbling.
examples: Critics dismissed him as a dilettante who painted only on weekends.
She was no dilettante; she had studied the subject for decades.

words.definition: a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds
words.nuance: Also used figuratively for clashing voices.
examples: The cacophony of car horns woke the whole street.
A cacophony of opinions drowned out the facts.

words.definition: a thing belonging to a period other than that in which it exists
words.nuance: Either a historical error or something old-fashioned.
examples: The wristwatch in the medieval film was an obvious anachronism.
The typewriter on his desk seemed an anachronism.

words.definition: a division or contrast between two things that are opposed or entirely different
words.nuance: Often questioned as a false dichotomy.
examples: The novel explores the dichotomy between duty and desire.
Some scholars reject the dichotomy of nature versus nurture.

words.definition: peculiar to an individual; distinctive or eccentric
words.nuance: A personal quirk rather than a flaw.
examples: The author's idiosyncratic spelling annoyed his editors.
Each judge has an idiosyncratic way of running the courtroom.

words.definition: uninterested in cultures, ideas, or peoples outside one's own experience
words.nuance: From the Latin for island: cut off.
examples: The insular community distrusted outsiders.
Critics called the department insular and resistant to new ideas.

words.definition: having a limited or narrow outlook or scope
words.nuance: Also refers to a church parish, as in parochial schools.
examples: The debate was dominated by parochial concerns about local parking.
His parochial view of the world ended when he moved abroad.

words.definition: unsophisticated or narrow-minded, especially as attributed to people outside a capital
words.nuance: Also the neutral meaning 'of a province'.
examples: The city's art scene was dismissed as provincial.
Her provincial attitudes changed after college.

words.definition: having developed certain abilities at an earlier age than usual
words.nuance: Can be admiring or slightly critical (too grown-up).
examples: The precocious child was reading novels at age four.
Her precocious talent for chess drew national attention.
